properties.decision: Of the four roads the XRPL-amendment idea laid out, take (a) — widen the stamp — but SCOPED TO ENUM VALUES ONLY. The stamp now records every enum vocabulary the schema declares, keyed Type.property; the guard compares them on open and refuses only when the graph actually STORES a value this binary does not know, naming the value. Property additions are deliberately NOT recorded. Semantic changes are deliberately NOT claimed to be caught. Roads (b) per-change identities, (c) severity per change and (d) nothing are not taken, for the reasons below.
properties.name: PROPOSED — the version guard widens to ENUM VALUES and stops there: property additions and semantic changes stay outside any structural fingerprint
properties.rationale:
THE THREE CLASSES ARE NOT EQUALLY HARMFUL, and that is what decides the scope. An ENUM VALUE is the severe one: Decision.status gaining `deferred` moves no count and no name, an older binary opens the graph with no warning, compares status == "proposed", and the decision does not error — it VANISHES from loop_status and what_next. That is the exact harm the guard's own refusal names. A PROPERTY ADDITION makes an older reader show fewer fields, which it can already tell, and mis-filters nothing; this project adds properties constantly (the fourteen-holes work alone), so recording them would turn nearly every release into a migration for a harm that is "you saw less". A SEMANTIC CHANGE — a field's meaning moved while its name did not — is beyond any structural fingerprint, so widening the stamp further would not reach it and claiming otherwise would be the overstating failure.

WHY NOT (b), per-change identities: it is a registry somebody maintains forever, and its failure mode is a change that lands without an entry — at which point the guard actively asserts the graph is fine. This project has already found that a retirement is two edits, not one, with RETIRED_NODE_TYPES. Semantic changes are the only class that NEEDS (b), and they are rare enough that the registry's cost is not yet earned. It stays open.

WHY NOT (c), severity per change: somebody has to classify each change, and the incentive at the moment of classifying is always the cheaper severity. The population probe already gives the honest form of severity for free — a declared value nobody stores is no severity at all.

WHY NOT (d), nothing: the probe only works for what the stamp NAMES, and before this it could not name an enum value.

THE TENSION WITH THE STAMP'S OWN REASON FOR BEING SMALL — "it must not depend on the vocabulary it is describing" — is real and was answered rather than routed around: the stamp already names types, which are vocabulary; enum values are the same kind of fact one level finer, the field is `#[serde(default)]` so every older stamp still parses, and the values do not enter content_hash, so lineage is untouched. Size is a few hundred short strings.

ONE HONEST LIMIT, stated in the code where it lives: reflow2 keeps no registry of REMOVED enum values, so when a graph holds a value this binary lacks the guard cannot say whether the binary is behind or the value was removed. It names both possibilities and hands the reader the only discriminator there is — the two stamps' own versions — rather than asserting the commoner case and being confidently wrong on the day somebody removes a value. When that day comes, the fix is the registry types already have.

SEQUENCED BEFORE dec/req:an-idea-that-stopped-is-not-counted-as-debt on Anthony's word (2026-09-11, "go with your suggested order"), because that increment adds exactly the enum value this guard could not see.
